questions.q: Why does the lesson say AI champions should get a couple of hours of protected time each week?
options: Volunteer enthusiasm fades quickly without protected time
Champions must approve every prompt before anyone uses it
Champions need the time to run all four training sessions alone
It lets champions review every AI output the team sends out
questions.explain: The lesson says to give champions a couple of hours of protected time each week because volunteer enthusiasm fades quickly without it. Their role is to answer questions, maintain the prompt library, run show-and-tells and collect feedback.

questions.q: At a 12-person insurance brokerage, an experienced account manager asks, "Will this replace me?" What does the lesson suggest the owner do?
options: Promise that nobody's role will ever change, whatever happens
Share the intent, the tasks targeted and how freed-up time will be used
Put off the conversation until the training sessions are finished
Point out that AI makes mistakes, so it couldn't really replace anyone
questions.explain: The lesson's honest response is to share your intent, show which tasks you're targeting and explain how freed-up time will be used. If roles will change, say how, because honesty builds more trust than reassurance.

questions.q: A dental practice manager is planning hands-on AI practice for the front-desk team. Which approach does the lesson recommend?
options: Use last week's real patient emails so the practice feels authentic
Skip practice and show one long demo of everything AI can do
Use realistic but fictional material, like AI-written practice exercises
Let each person practice alone on whatever tasks they happen to pick
questions.explain: The lesson says practice works best with realistic but fictional material, so nobody is tempted to paste real customer data while learning. It includes a prompt that creates exercises with fictional sample input.
